title: SARAH LOOKED AT HAGAR’S SON AND SAID, “SEND THEM AWAY”—BUT WHAT GOD DID IN THE DESERT CHANGES HOW YOU READ THE ENTIRE STORY
paragraphs: SARAH LOOKED AT HAGAR’S SON AND SAID, “SEND THEM AWAY”—BUT WHAT GOD DID IN THE DESERT CHANGES HOW YOU READ THE ENTIRE STORY

The heartbreaking story of Sarah, Abraham, Hagar, Ishmael, and Isaac is not merely about a broken household. It exposes what happens when human beings try to manufacture what God promised—and reveals the astonishing mercy of the God who still hears people crying in the wilderness.
There are sentences in the Bible that are difficult to read slowly.
This is one of them.
Sarah looked at Abraham—the man who had waited decades with her for the promised child—and demanded that another woman and Abraham’s own son be sent away.
Not relocated.
Not given another room.
Sent away.
The Hebrew of Genesis 21:10 is painfully direct:
גָּרֵשׁ הָאָמָה הַזֹּאת וְאֶת־בְּנָהּ
Gāresh hā’āmāh hazzō’t we’et-benāh.
“Drive out this servant woman and her son.”
Then Sarah gives the reason.
כִּי לֹא יִירַשׁ בֶּן־הָאָמָה הַזֹּאת עִם־בְּנִי עִם־יִצְחָק
“For the son of this servant woman shall not inherit with my son, with Isaac.”
Those words tore through Abraham.
Scripture does not portray him as emotionally untouched.
Genesis says:
וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָר מְאֹד בְּעֵינֵי אַבְרָהָם עַל אוֹדֹת בְּנוֹ
The matter was exceedingly grievous in Abraham’s eyes...
because of his son.
That last phrase matters.
Ishmael was not an inconvenience to Abraham.
He was his son.
Before Isaac ever laughed inside Abraham’s tent, Ishmael had called Abraham father.
Before Isaac took his first steps, Abraham had watched Ishmael grow.
Abraham had held him.
Loved him.
Circumcised him in obedience to God.
And when God previously told Abraham that Sarah would bear the covenant son, Abraham himself cried:
“Oh that Ishmael might live before You!”
There was a father underneath the patriarch.
And now that father was being torn apart.
But to understand why this family reached such a devastating morning, you have to go backward.
Because Hagar did not simply appear in Abraham’s story.
She entered the story when faith became tired of waiting.
God had promised Abraham descendants.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
And eventually the silence between promise and fulfillment became unbearable.
So Sarah devised another way.
Genesis 16 records that Sarah gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham so that a child might be obtained through her.
And Abraham agreed.
That decision is one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable mirrors because we still do the same thing.
God speaks.
We believe Him.
Then nothing seems to happen.
Days become months.
Months become years.
Prayer begins to feel like talking into an empty room.
And somewhere between “God promised” and “God fulfilled,” we become tempted to help God accomplish what only God can accomplish.
We manufacture.
Manipulate.
Force doors.
Compromise convictions.
Choose relationships God never gave us.
Create shortcuts.
Call impatience “wisdom.”
Call fear “being realistic.”
And sometimes we even attach God’s name to decisions that were born from our inability to wait for Him.
Abraham and Sarah had received a promise.
But Hagar became entangled in their attempt to produce through human strength what God intended to accomplish through divine faithfulness.
Then Hagar conceived Ishmael.
And suddenly what looked like a solution became a household wound.
There was resentment.
Humiliation.
Conflict.
Hagar fled.
And this is where something astonishing happened.
The woman caught inside Abraham and Sarah’s broken decision ran into the wilderness...
and God went looking for her.
Genesis 16 says the Angel of the LORD found her near a spring.
Think about that.
Hagar was an Egyptian servant.
Socially vulnerable.
Pregnant.
Running.
Hurting.
Probably wondering whether anyone in the world cared what happened to her.
But heaven knew her location.
God called her by name.
“Hagar.”
And God told her that the child inside her would be named:
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma‘el.
Ishmael.
The name is built around the Hebrew verb שָׁמַע — shāma‘, “to hear.”
His name carried a message:
God hears.
The biblical explanation is explicit: the LORD had heard Hagar’s affliction.
Imagine carrying that name through life.
Every time Hagar called her son—
“Ishmael!”
—she was repeating the testimony of the wilderness.
God hears.
Dinner is ready, God-hears.
Come home, God-hears.
Stay close to me, God-hears.
My son...
God heard me.
And Hagar responded to this encounter with one of the most moving confessions in Genesis.
She spoke of the God who saw her.
The invisible servant had discovered that she was not invisible to heaven.
Remember that when you feel overlooked.
Remember Hagar when everyone seems to have continued living while you are barely surviving.
Remember her when your prayers seem trapped beneath the ceiling.
Remember her when someone else's decisions created wounds you never asked to carry.
Human beings may overlook you.
People may use you.
Families may fail you.
Someone may put you in a situation you never chose and then leave you carrying the consequences.
But you have never disappeared from God's sight.
Years passed.
Then God did what human strength could never do.
Sarah conceived.
Isaac was born.
The impossible child arrived.
The promised son laughed inside Abraham’s house.
And eventually Sarah saw Ishmael מְצַחֵק — metzaḥeq.

The Hebrew word comes from the same root associated with laughter and Isaac’s name. English translations render the scene differently, including ideas such as laughing, playing, or mocking; the precise nuance has been debated. The New Testament later interprets the conflict in Galatians 4:29 in terms of the son born according to the flesh persecuting the son associated with God’s promise.
Sarah responded:
Send the servant woman away.
Send her son away.
And Abraham was devastated.
Then God spoke.
This is where careless readings of the story can become dangerous.
God did not tell Abraham that Ishmael was worthless.
God did not say Hagar was invisible.
God did not suddenly forget the woman He had previously found beside the spring.
Instead, God reaffirmed that His covenant line would be reckoned through Isaac while simultaneously promising concerning Ishmael:
“I will make a nation of the son of the servant woman also, because he is your offspring.”
Isaac had a particular covenant role.
Ishmael still remained under God's providential care.
Those truths must not be confused.
God's election of Isaac for the covenant promise was not a declaration that Ishmael possessed no human worth.
Then morning came.
Abraham rose early.
There was bread.
There was water.
There was Hagar.
There was Ishmael.
And there was goodbye.
Try not to rush through that scene.
Scripture gives us no sentimental soundtrack.
No lengthy recorded farewell speech.
Just Abraham preparing provisions...
and sending them away.
Hagar entered the wilderness of Beersheba.
Then the water ran out.
That sentence becomes terrifying when you are a mother in a wilderness.
No convenience store.
No emergency vehicle.
No hospital.
No phone.
No visible rescue.
Just heat.
Dust.
Thirst.
And your child dying in front of you.
Eventually Hagar could no longer bear watching.
She placed the boy beneath a shrub.
Then she walked away and sat at a distance.
Her reasoning was devastating:
Do not let me see the boy die.
Then she wept.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of prayer.
Not polished prayer.
Not church prayer.
Not the prayer where every theological phrase is perfectly arranged.
The prayer that sounds more like sobbing.
The prayer where you have run out of explanations.
The prayer whispered from a hospital corridor.
The prayer prayed beside divorce papers.
The prayer after the funeral.
The prayer when your child has wandered from God.
The prayer when the money is gone.
The prayer when addiction has returned.
The prayer when nobody knows how exhausted you actually are.
The prayer where all you have left is:
And tears.
Then Genesis says something breathtaking.
וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶת־קוֹל הַנַּעַר
Vayyishma Elohim et-qol hanna‘ar.
“God heard the voice of the boy.”
Do you see it?
His name was Ishmael.
God hears.
Years earlier, God had heard Hagar’s affliction.
Now in the wilderness, God heard the boy.
The name had become the story.
And the story had become testimony.
God hears.
When the water disappears...
God hears.
When the family breaks...
God hears.
When the future looks buried underneath a desert shrub...
God hears.
When your strength cannot produce another sentence...
God hears.
God called to Hagar and told her not to fear.
Then Scripture says:
“God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.”
Read that again.
The wilderness had convinced Hagar that death was the only ending available.
God opened her eyes...
and there was water.
Sometimes despair does that to us.
It narrows our vision until pain becomes the only thing we can see.
We begin believing the chapter we are living must be the final chapter.
The marriage failed, therefore everything is over.
The child wandered, therefore nothing can change.
I sinned, therefore God cannot use me.
I wasted years, therefore redemption has passed me by.
I ruined something beautiful, therefore grace has finally reached its limit.
But the Gospel announces something radically different.
Your worst chapter does not possess authorship over your final chapter.
Jesus does.
And this is where Sarah, Hagar, Isaac, and Ishmael ultimately confront something inside every one of us.
We want to save ourselves.
We want to produce the promise.
We want righteousness we can manufacture.
We want enough morality, enough religion, enough effort, enough reputation, enough church attendance, enough spiritual achievement to make ourselves acceptable before God.
But Scripture keeps destroying that illusion.
Paul eventually reaches back into this very family tragedy in Galatians 4.
He speaks of Abraham's two sons and uses their story allegorically in his argument about slavery and freedom, flesh and promise.
Paul's point is not permission to despise Hagar or Ishmael.
Nor is it a justification for ethnic hostility.
His argument is theological.
Human effort cannot manufacture the freedom God gives by promise.
And that brings us directly to Jesus Christ.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people finally tried hard enough to reach God.
It is the announcement that God came for people who could not rescue themselves.
Jesus entered our wilderness.
He stepped into human rejection.
He knew betrayal.
He knew abandonment.
He knew what it meant to be despised.
And at the cross, the sinless Son of God carried sins that were not His.
Our pride.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our secret compromises.
Our religious hypocrisy.
Our manipulation.
Our impatience.
Our attempts to control what should have been surrendered.
Our hidden browser history.
Our private hatred.
Our unforgiveness.
Our self-righteousness.
Our rebellion.
Our shame.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
And there He died.
Not as a tragic victim trapped by history...
but as the Lamb of God giving Himself for sinners.
Then the grave received Him.
And the grave could not keep Him.
Jesus Christ rose.
That changes everything.
Because perhaps the deepest wilderness is not Hagar's desert.
It is the distance sin created between humanity and God.
And we cannot manufacture enough water to escape it.
We cannot perform our way out.
We cannot religiously decorate our chains and call ourselves free.
We need grace.
We need forgiveness.
We need Christ.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so much.
There is a little Abraham in us—trying to control what God promised.
There is something of Sarah's impatience in us—hurting people while trying to protect what we fear losing.
There is something of Hagar's wilderness in us—wondering whether anybody sees.
There is something of Ishmael's cry in us—needing God to hear.
And there is only one Savior standing above all of it.
Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years blaming everyone else for the wilderness while refusing to confront the decisions that helped bring you there.
Maybe you were the wounded person.
Maybe you were the person who caused the wound.
Maybe somehow you have been both.
The Gospel has room for that confession.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Christ who died and rose to redeem sinners.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace tells the truth about evil...
then reveals a Savior greater than our sin.
That is why you do not need to hide anymore.
Bring Christ the resentment.
Bring Him the jealousy.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the secret addiction.
Bring Him the marriage you damaged.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the bitterness you have carefully justified.
Bring Him the religious mask.
Bring Him the wilderness.
Bring Him the empty water skin.
Bring Him the thing underneath the shrub that you have already decided cannot survive.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
Someone reading silently tonight may need to discover that deserts are not always graves.
Not because every sentence is easy.
God hears.
Not as religious decoration.
Even send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know that Jesus still receives sinners.
Supporting Gospel ministry is never a purchase of God's favor. We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, service, and lives surrendered to Him.
If you want to support Gospel Warrior and go deeper with us:
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because perhaps someone in your world is currently sitting beside an empty water skin.
Someone is crying where nobody can hear them.
Someone thinks their scandal became their identity.
Someone believes the mistake they made fifteen years ago wrote the ending.
Someone thinks the wilderness proves God abandoned them.
Someone needs to hear the ancient name again:
יִשְׁמָעֵאל.
Yishma‘el.
God hears.
And someone needs to hear an even greater name:
Jesus.
The One who saves His people from their sins.
Sarah could demand that Hagar leave.
Abraham could send her into the wilderness.
The water could run out.
Hagar could lose sight of hope.
But none of them could send Hagar beyond the reach of God.
And neither can your past send you beyond the reach of Christ.
Not your scandal.
Not your shame.
Not your failure.
Not the wilderness.
Not the years you lost.
Not the chapter you wish you could tear out of your life.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive the mercy you could never manufacture for yourself.
And when Christ has rewritten what sin tried to make permanent, do not hide the testimony.
Follow and stay close to the Word.
Support the mission if God has given you the desire and means to do so.
Then go tell another thirsty soul where the living water is found.
Because perhaps the most beautiful truth buried inside this painful family story is this:
When human failure sends someone into the wilderness, God can still meet them there—and the desert does not get to write the final sentence.
